title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced one shared initial candidate per task with gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the identical candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could invoke ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline successes = 120/120; guarded successes = 120/120; contingency: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false in all guarded episodes. We address peer-review requests by (1) condensing provenance into a compact artifact paragraph, (2) providing a compact formal scoring-rule mapping scorer/validator fields to the binary pass/fail outcome with a concrete archived example, and (3) adding a nearest-work comparison matrix contrasting how this design differs from the closest prior studies.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can convert operator intent into device-level configuration commands, but syntactically plausible outputs can violate workflow invariants (for example, make-before-break requirements or required shutdown-before-MTU-change), producing semantic failures that only appear in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore recommends adding verification, emulation, or digital-twin checks and bounded repair loops before enactment. Our preregistered confirmatory question (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) asks: does integrating an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate the validator/repair marginal effect we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: for each task a single generator output was scored both as baseline (LLM-only) and as guarded (validator ± repair). The principal contribution is a preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) that demonstrates how a shared-generation design cleanly isolates validator effects and how deterministic archival traces facilitate reproducible failure analysis even when the primary test is degenerate.
sections.related_work:
Executable closed-loop benchmarks and NetOps verification work emphasize that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment; emulation reveals sequencing and stateful errors that syntactic checks miss. Tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) are proposed and prototype-evaluated as safety measures. However, systematic closed-loop comparisons that (a) hold generator outputs fixed while measuring validator/repair effects, and (b) provide deterministic reconciliation artifacts, remain limited. Nearest-work comparison (concise matrix):

- Protogeros et al., "Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair" (arXiv:2604.22513): benchmark and repair evaluation; focuses on generator/repair performance but not a shared-generation paired isolation of validator marginal effects. Differences: this study uses shared-generation paired design and deterministic reconciliation; Protogeros et al. emphasize multi-draw generator evaluation and repair behavior under independent sampling.

- Liu et al., "NetConfArena" (arXiv:2608.23179): executable closed-loop benchmark using emulation; exposes semantic failures in closed-loop runs. Differences: NetConfArena evaluates closed-loop behavior across generator variability; our paired design holds generator output fixed to isolate validator/repair marginal effect.

- Augé et al., "Aether: Network Validation Using Agentic AI and Digital Twin" (arXiv:2604.18233): argues for digital-twin based validation and agentic workflows. Differences: Aether presents agentic integration and digital-twin prototypes; our work provides a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic artifact reconciliation and an explicit repair-budget arm (≤1 repair).

- Zhou et al., "MeshAgent: Enabling Reliable Network Management with Large Language Models" (SIG reference): proposes reliability mechanisms and guardrails for LLM-driven NetOps. Differences: MeshAgent focuses on architecture and empirical evaluation under varied prompts; our contribution is a preregistered paired statistical test that isolates validator effects with complete archival accountability.

- Tang et al., "Lightyear" (BGP verification): formal verification emphasis for control-plane correctness. Differences: Lightyear focuses on scalable formal verification; our study experimentally measures the empirical effect of an executable validator plus bounded repair on generated configuration candidates under a shared-generation protocol.

This matrix shows the complementary experiment/architectural axes: (shared-generation paired vs independent-generation), (executable emulator validator vs syntactic/formal checks), (repair budget and policy), and (task corpus provenance). Our run occupies the validator-marginal isolation point with deterministic archival instrumentation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. We preregistered CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 before execution. Design: paired-binary confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks deterministic-partitioned into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine; 40 tasks each). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact two-sided McNemar; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair budget: ≤1 repair per guarded episode. Planned episodes = 240 (baseline+guarded per pair); completed episodes = 240. Model scope declared: gpt-5-mini.

Task generation and structured payload. Tasks were produced deterministically (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, and a canonical required_sequence (ordered operations). Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) enable targeted stratification in future work.

Shared-generation paired protocol. For each task we performed a single shared initial candidate generation using gpt-5-mini (execution manifest: model_calls_used = 120; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}). The identical generated candidate was scored in both conditions to isolate validator/repair effects from generator variance. The trade-off: if the generator yields valid candidates for the selected task bank, the guardian cannot exercise repair — an anticipated risk in the preregistration.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), which executes the candidate in an emulator and enforces structured workflow policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator emits a structured validator_trace containing validation_before/after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count > 0; repair prompts and traces were archived when produced. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 across all guarded episodes and no repair artifacts were generated.

Compact artifact paragraph (condensed provenance). All execution and analysis artifacts required to reproduce the confirmatory accounting are archived in the study artifact bundle. Representative items include: raw_results and provider traces (execution/raw_results), the deterministic task manifest (execution/task_manifest), the model configuration record declaring gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration), representative scorer/validator JSONs (execution/scoring/*), the paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv), condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv), and deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). Long provenance inventories and per-file hashes have been relocated to the archived artifact bundle and the supplementary reconciliation artifact; readers may consult those archived artifacts for exact filenames and checksums. (This paragraph replaces earlier inline provenance listings to improve narrative flow while preserving machine-verifiable artifacts in the bundle.)

Formal binary scoring rule (compact). We used a deterministic decision rule mapping archived scorer/validator fields to the binary pass/fail label used in the McNemar test. Binary outcome = PASS if and only if all of the following hold in the scorer/validator artifacts for an episode: (1) scoring_status == "COMPLETED"; (2) scorer.score == 1 (score reason "VALID_CONFIGURATION"); and (3) validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count == 0. Otherwise the episode is labeled FAIL. Tie-breaking: episodes with technical/instrumentation failure or missing scorer/validator fields are excluded per the preregistration (none occurred here). Concrete archived example (pass): execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows scoring_status = "COMPLETED", score = 1, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count = 0; therefore this episode is labeled PASS under the formal rule. The same rule was applied uniformly to baseline and guarded episodes to produce the paired contingency table used in the confirmatory analysis.

Instrumentation and contamination controls. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets (container image checksums + deterministic seeds) and applied contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse). Provider-call audits and deterministic reconciliation artifacts ensure internal accounting consistency. The execution manifest reports: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 120; maximum_model_calls = 240; start/completion timestamps are recorded in the archived manifest.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions: completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Condition-level summaries record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; consequently preregistered secondary endpoints quantifying repair incidence are vacuous here.

Per-topology counts. Tasks were deterministically partitioned with 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology outcomes are: Edge: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40. These counts are recorded in analysis/condition_summary.csv and the representative scoring JSONs archived (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json).

Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts show normalized_response == normalized_reference_answer; parsed_command_count == required_command_count; validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true; repair_applied == false; validator_id == deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator_version == 5.0. The observed canonical required_sequences (for example, shut→configure→restore) were satisfied by the generator outputs under the frozen prompt strategy, explaining the absence of violations.

Contamination, missingness, and reconciliation. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero technical/instrumentation exclusions. analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms internal accounting consistency (n_11 = 120; hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and implications. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by removing generator variance across paired episodes. In this curated task bank and with the frozen prompt configuration the generator produced valid candidates for every task; consequently the guarded pipeline was never required to apply repair and could not improve upon the baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical reflections of this ceiling outcome.

Design trade-offs and recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but may under-exercise repair when generators are well-calibrated for the task bank. To measure repair utility in future confirmatory runs we recommend preregistered adjustments: (1) independent per-condition generation or blocked randomization so guarded arms can intercept generator-induced errors; (2) targeted selection of tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count to increase generator-error incidence; (3) prespecified prompt perturbations on a controlled subset to elevate generator variability while retaining paired controls; (4) exploratory arms permitting >1 repair iteration to measure convergence and repair costs. The archived task_manifest difficulty fields support targeted follow-up selection without changing harness semantics.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by task encoding and validator policy coverage; the emulator enforces structured checks derived from synthetic payloads and does not capture all vendor-specific or telemetry-limited failure modes. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and the frozen prompt strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power assumptions (baseline ≈0.40, target absolute reduction 0.15) were violated by the observed baseline = 0.00, rendering the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.

Reproducibility. All primary execution and analysis artifacts required to reproduce the confirmatory accounting are archived in the study artifact bundle (representative names given above). The analysis log records bootstrap parameters (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). The archived deterministic_reconciliation artifact demonstrates provider-call accounting and pair-consistency checks. These artifacts support deterministic replay of the paired analysis and targeted follow-ups that relax the shared-generation constraint or concentrate on high-difficulty tasks.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the emulator validator, producing n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and illustrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask potential repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our methodological contribution is twofold: (1) we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects; and (2) we show how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. Archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax shared-generation constraints, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this design choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
